column1: Mimicking

Can you describe the smelliest person you have met? The first time I met Mr. Smelly I thought it was an act of Divine Intervention. Or perhaps a premonition. It was back in my early teens, and like many of the other students in my school, I was an unmotivated teenager. I was in the final year of my secondary education and I had little motivation for just about anything. My life consisted of going to school, attempting to flirt with girls, and listening to music. I was obsessed with heavy metal and gothic rock, something that wasn't even remotely cool in Trinidad and Tobago in the early 2000s. I also spent most of my time playing video games, particularly games on the PlayStation. Much to my chagrin I never got any of the things that the cool kids had back then. I had no money, a meager social life, and most of the girls at school either ignored me or made fun of me. So rather than spend time studying for school, I would often miss classes and go to the cinema. It was at the cinema that I first encountered Mr. Smelly. I was very late for a movie and I ran inside in a disheveled, sweaty and stressed state to barely make it for the start of the trailers. As I took my seat, a distinct, powerful and foul stench penetrated my nostrils. I looked around and it seemed I was the only person offended by it. The few students that were in attendance didn't seem to care and the other patrons merely seemed to be unfazed. I couldn't tell where the smell was coming from. It could have been the stale, filthy seats; the ancient, poorly maintained air conditioning system or perhaps it was a member of the audience. I ignored it at first. I told myself the smell would go away. But throughout the entire movie, the smell, which I can only describe as the combination of putrid seafood and old urine, lingered in the air. I found myself unable to fully enjoy the film. During the climactic scenes, I was more concerned with whether the stench was getting worse or not. The movie ended, and as the patrons left, the smell seemed to disperse. I was happy. As I exited the cinema I made a mental note to return home straight away and take a shower. As I was heading out the exit a large, unkempt man with a greasy, long-sleek hair, unshaven face and torn, stained clothes walked past. He was smiling. In that instant, the smell manifested again. I realized then that the smell was neither the seats nor the air conditioning. It was him. I averted my eyes and walked away. I made a mental note to never return to the same cinema again. I later learned that Mr. Smelly, who wasn’t a student at my school, was a somewhat regular fixture at the cinema and a somewhat local annoyance. As the years passed the memory of Mr. Smelly faded. I often forgot about him, as one usually does with awkward and embarrassing memories from their youth. But that wasn't the final time I encountered Mr. Smelly. Far from it. Over the years fate seemed to bring us face to face more than a few times, often in the most inconvenient locations. Each time the stench would return. And so would my profound displeasure.

What’s the most unprofessional thing a doctor has said to you? "Thing? You mean things. If you trust the word of just one doctor here in Trinidad you already have one foot (or in our case, leg) in the grave. My ex and I witnessed the not so great morals and ethics of some of the private health care 'professionals’ in Trinidad after she developed a severe case of cellulitis. This developed after she suffered a cut from a dirty galvanize sheet a neighbor had lying about in the road. This is how it looked after a month of healing. You don’t want to see what it looked like when it was critical. The disrespectful and dishonest negligence of the doctors who treated her was far worse than the actual injury. Left up to them, she could’ve lost her leg or gotten blood poisoning and die. So what did the doctors do/say? Here’s what happened: The cut looked minor so she decided to ignore it. A few days later an infection spreads around it the size of closed fist and it burns her all day. She had the typical Trini mindset that the public hospitals were were no good so I took her to a private doctor her relatives recommended. Said doctor diagnosed the infection as a mild case of cellulitis, gives her a prescription for some weak pills and sends us off. A week later the infection spreads to the size of a man’s foot and it burns even more severely. In panic we visit another private doctor and he tells us something to the extent of: ‘It’s just a minor infection. It’s just running its course.’ He bandages her leg and prescribes her the same medication like the last doctor. He bashes the last doctor for not bandaging her leg. We return to the old doctor to give him a piece of our mind and get our money back. His curmudgeonous, old secretary tells us that the doctor is busy. We show her the extent to which the infection has spread and she replies: ‘So what? It’s not like her leg is rotten.’ Tempted to choke slam the old bitch I take my rage out on the door and in a mad fury I threaten that I would come back to smear s**t all over his office building during the night…..because that what they really were. We place our trust in the second doctor and visit him weekly even though all he does is re-bandage her leg and prescribe the same medicine. He keeps assuring us that cellulitis is common and non-threatening, not to worry. At this point the infection has spread throughout her entire leg. The new doctor is collecting a neat $500 from me for each visit. By the third visit, he unwraps the old bandages and I literally see him gulp in shock as he witnesses the extent of the infection. I’ll never forget the cheap smile on the smug face as he tries to play it off coolly by saying: ‘Ok……it seems to have spread a bit. Maybe if I prescribe a stronger medication?’ That was when I realized the scheme. Some private doctors make their wealth by prolonging the ailment. Took her immediately to our Mt. Hope public hospital where she was confined for several days. The doctor there told her that if we had continued in the manner in which we treated the situation, best case scenario would’ve been an amputated leg. I shuddered when she recalled to me those words. I can only imagine the amount of lives lost due to selfish, negligent doctors looking to profit off of people’s misfortunes. The scar remains on her leg, not as prominent, but as a subtle reminder to a) Do not take any injury for granted, regardless how minor. b) Just because it’s private i.e. non Governmental, doesn’t mean it’s better. Edit 21.01.22. Sorry if this answer was a bit depressing. Have you ever been depressed? I survived a really bad spell myself. Thankfully I lived through it and was lucky that it was not clinical. Click here to read all about it.

Why do women *hate* nerdy men? When I was coming into my teens I was a proper nerd. I was obsessed with Japanese anime, foreign films, the 60s and the psychedelic rock of the period. When I wasn't writing my pompous and psudo-artsy short stories I was spending hours behind the PlayStation and computer playing video games. When I wasn't watching late night soft-core porn on Cinemax I was delighting in clips from the Classical Arts Showcase channel. I would rant and vent about how awful the girls in my school were to the girls in my school. I would find solace in the public library where I scoured the building looking for that quiet, introverted pretty young girl(s) from an all girls school and would proceed to sit next to her(them) without asking permission and then I would gush about my unfinished surreal novel about a country boy in my class having trouble deciphering dreams from reality and vice versa. These girls would find me mildly amusing and interesting but I didn't seem to understand that 'Sorry my parents don't allow me to give out our phone number is actually a diplomatic way of saying no. (This was before cell phones were a thing.) Yes I was a nerd. A big nerd. I still am. However girls didn't hate the nerd in me. What they didn't like was that: Those behaviors had a hint of the creepy about them. It felt as though if one dared to stare into my eyes, the eyes of your classic “nerd,” they might get a glimpse into a soul that had been through the ninth circle of hell. Nerds can be annoying but harmless. As an awkward adolescent with no friends and a bad case of acne, I couldn't understand what girls wanted. I thought my extensive knowledge of the Lord of the Rings trilogy and my encyclopedic understanding of the works of David Lynch and Antonioni were enough to woo any one of those, so-called, beautiful girls. They were not. And they never would be. The girls didn’t *hate* me. They hated the signs of possible narcissists, self-centred a**holes, crybabies and sociopaths. Not that I was any of the above it’s just that those are the type of men girls really *hate* and even fear. Not nerds so much.

What movies have you judged just by looking at their posters? Something about this poster just rubbed me the wrong way. Is that a movie or a shot of the celebrity audience during the last Academy Awards? At first glance it looks like the typical dime-a-dozen Hollywood movie poster. The kind of movie poster that would fleetingly catch your fancy if you're late to the cinema and the movie you wanted to watch is sold out. But when you actually sit and and digest the vision before you, you might be like me and notice it has ALL the trappings of a tepid Hollywood wannabe blockbuster. The poster seems to scream several things to you all at once: Despite the little information that is given, you have an idea of what the gist of the movie is about. None of the above posters are hiding their story behind a montage of A-list faces. All the above posters are proud of their story and want you to know what you are paying to see. Either through clever visuals or teasing, enigmatic catch phrases, you have an idea whether this movie is your cup of tea or not. Let's take a look at the poster for *Don't Look Up* one last time. That’s just rancid. Adam McKay and his major studio goons insult my intelligence by telling me that I'm too stupid to understand satire so rather than waste time hinting what the story is about, here are a bunch of eye pleasing celebrities…..and it's inspired by stuff that might kinda happen. I'm not gonna see this movie based on this poster. I might be missing the greatest film of the 21st century but I'll trust my intuition on this one. Edit 10.01.22. Geez, what an awful poster. Do you judge a movie by its poster? Click here to see my pick of the greatest and worst movie poster I’ve ever seen.

What is the lowest probability event you have personally witnessed? "Unbelievable," I thought to myself, "Can this really be happening again?" A sense of impending doom washed over me. I could feel a wave of resignation creeping in. The probability of this event -- this **exact** event -- happening again was astronomically small. Forget about winning the lottery, this was in another realm of impossibility. I was flummoxed. I could not believe my eyes. Having already once experienced Gandhi's incessant chatter for six whole hours during the course of a cross country trip, the prospect of enduring a second experience of such a cataclysmic ordeal was too much to bear. As if the universe had a vendetta against my sanity. I was resigned to my fate. The irony of it all was almost comical. Of all the people in the world, and across two vastly different locations (Dominica and back in Trinidad), I had, once again, landed myself beside my acquaintance and tormentor. This time in a different country, on a different journey and on a different bus. It felt almost like a cruel joke. A cosmic prank orchestrated by some unseen force. I struggled to maintain a modicum of composure and, bracing myself. The monotonous drone began.

What's your take on Imane Khelif, a biologically proven male boxer, taking part in the Women's Boxing event at the Paris Olympics 2024? This whole controversy stirs a cauldron of complex feelings within me, a veritable storm of ethical considerations and practical worries. On the surface, the issue seems straightforward: a biological male competing in a women's sporting event. Yet, as is often the case in realms of identity, fairness, and inclusion the reality soon dissolves into a murky abyss of nuanced considerations. My initial reaction is one of unease, a knot of apprehension that tightens as I consider the immense disparity in physical attributes between biological males and females; the obvious advantage. Boxing, at its core, is a brutal game of controlled violence, where the slightest difference in strength, speed, and stamina can spell victory or defeat. To allow a biological male, regardless of hormone therapy or reassignment, to compete against women seems, frankly, like a grave injustice. It’s a violation of the very spirit of competition, potentially endangering female athletes at a time when women have fought so hard to get a space in a world which has always been overwhelmingly dominated by men. However, the situation is hardly black and white. There are those who champion Khelif's inclusion, arguing for the rights of transgender individuals to participate fully in society, including sports. They point out the inherent discrimination in excluding someone based on their identity, especially when hormone therapy has supposedly reduced the advantages conferred by a male body. The idea of creating separate categories for trans athletes further complicates matters. How far would one be required to accommodate someone's truth? Where do these borders begin and end? This is why I understand the arguments on both sides. And as I mentioned earlier, those are the type of debates that one truly understands how complex topics can get. Where does the line get drawn? Where can one find a balance between fairness, safety, and the right to feel validated in their truths? When the time comes Imane Khelif’s place in the 2024 Olympics, the sport of boxing risks turning into a symbolic battleground, where the clash of ideologies will be as fierce as any punch thrown in the ring.

Has your friend ever saved your life? Not in any literal sense, thankfully. My friends have frequently saved me from various degrees of embarrassment, which, let’s be honest, can be just as mortifying and sometimes more difficult to bounce back from than a near-death experience. One friend, let’s call him Kevin because, well, that’s his name, has a particular knack for rescuing me from social catastrophes. Kevin possesses an almost preternatural ability to sense when a social interaction is on the verge of imploding. He has the uncanny ability to interject with a timely joke, a well-placed distraction, or a sudden, urgent summons that allows me to escape a conversational quagmire unscathed.  There was that time I found myself trapped in a conversation at a party, cornered by this woman who was relentlessly talking about her cats. I am, as a matter of fact, not a cat person. After an uninterrupted half-hour of detailed descriptions of flea infestations and the peculiar habits of her feline companions, I could feel my sanity slipping. I was desperately searching for a non-offensive exit strategy, but the cat lady was like a psychological terminator. I was completely trapped. Just when I thought I would be subjected to another hour of unsolicited cat anecdotes, Kevin swooped in, feigning a panicked expression, and loudly announced, “Elijah! I need your help immediately! Remember that thing we were supposed to do? It’s now or never!” And that, folks, was my miraculous escape.  Then there was the incident with the karaoke. After a couple of adult beverages, I, regrettably, volunteered to perform. The song was some horrendous, power ballad. My voice is not what I’d consider a gift from the muses, and my rendition was disastrous. As bad was it could be. I butchered every single note. In fact, I was so bad, I was quickly becoming that spectacle everyone remembers and regrets the next morning. Seeing my impending humiliation, Kevin, without a moment’s hesitation, jumped up on stage and started doing the most outlandish, over-the-top dance moves whilst simultaneously grabbing the microphone. He began to sing along out of key even louder than I, effectively drawing all the attention away from my audible malpractice. It was the most selfless act of friendship I’ve ever witnessed. He saved me from myself, and the memory of what would have been a lifetime karaoke shame was averted.  So no, my friends have never saved my life from any physical danger. But they sure as hell have come to the rescue often enough to make me believe that they have, in a sense, salvaged my dignity on numerous occasions. And that, in my book, is a life-saving endeavor in its own right.

Have you ever had a life-changing experience while working in fast food? My first job, and one of the most formative, was at a prominent fast-food chain in town. I was a callow, rather clueless teenager, still grappling with the world outside of the confines of school and home. My primary motivation for taking on the role was simple: money. I needed cash for the latest video games, the newest albums from my favorite rock bands, and, of course, the occasional cinema outing. Little did I understand that this menial job would become a crucible, forging experiences that would shape my perspective in ways I could never have imagined.  The initial days were a blur of frenetic activity. I was thrust into a world of searing fryers, demanding customers, and the constant, rhythmic hum of ceaseless productivity. It was a baptism of fire, and frankly, I nearly drowned at first. The speed and precision required weren't intuitive, and I fumbled often. I made countless mistakes that resulted in reprimands from the shift managers. But somehow, I began to adapt. Slowly, painstakingly, I mastered the art of efficiently assembling a burger, expertly portioning fries, and memorizing the ever-changing promotional menu. The job, though tedious, started to become second nature.  What proved to be the turning point wasn't the mastery of the trade. It was the interactions I began to have with my workmates and, surprisingly, the customers. My fellow employees, a diverse bunch of young men and women from every background and walk of life, became my friends. We'd share stories, swap jokes, and console each other during particularly challenging shifts that were often imbued with the usual workplace drama. Through them, I was learning how to navigate the complex social terrain of an office and I started to understand the value of teamwork, loyalty, and camaraderie. I was seeing realities I wasn't privy to before.

What are some bad movies that could have worked by just having a better screenplay? Ah, the cinematic graveyard. A place where potential masterpieces lie entombed, suffocated by the very thing that breathes life into a film: a compelling and well-crafted screenplay. There are countless movies that, despite boasting promising premises, big-name actors, or stunning visuals, ultimately crash and burn because the narrative simply isn't up to snuff. Let's be honest, we've all sat through a film, squirming in our seats, as the plot meandered, the dialogue felt clunky, and the characters behaved in ways that defied all logic. It's a painful experience.  One film that immediately springs to mind is a dystopian sci-fi flick that somehow managed to secure a top-tier ensemble cast. The visuals were stunning, the world-building was intricate, yet the story felt like a rambling, incoherent mess. The characters were either paper-thin archetypes or inconsistent messes, and the overarching plot was so convoluted that, by the time the credits rolled, you were left scratching your head, wondering what in the blue hell you had just witnessed. A rewrite, some clever dialogue tweaks, and some serious character development would have elevated the movie from a forgettable misfire to a cult classic. I’m fairly certain that the writers were in an alternate dimension.

What's the biggest anticlimax in movie history? For me, the biggest cinematic letdown has to be the grand reveal in M. Night Shyamalan's *The Village*. The film, much like the director's other ventures, traffics in the currency of suspense; the subtle build-up, the carefully laid breadcrumbs, the unnerving score designed to keep you on the edge of your seat. You anticipate, for the better part of the film, some horrifying creature lurking in the woods, a menacing presence that threatens the safety of the insular village. The villagers, we learn, have a pact with these creatures, a desperate bargain they uphold through rituals and fear. The film's trailers and marketing campaigns were masterful in their obfuscation, hinting at a supernatural thriller while keeping the true nature of the threat shrouded in mystery. And then, the reveal. The "creatures" aren't monsters, not supernatural beings from some dark realm, but rather…villagers in cloaks. They were an elaborate hoax, a carefully orchestrated deception meant to protect the village from the outside world. It wasn't just a twist; it was a narrative collapse, a deflation of tension so complete that the audience was left reeling. The film, up to that point, had played with the tropes of horror and suspense, but the reveal itself was more akin to a Scooby-Doo episode, a narrative trick lacking the thematic depth and the psychological resonance that Shyamalan often strives for. The film was beautifully shot, with a score that was undeniably effective - but the resolution felt cheap and unsatisfying. All the carefully constructed tension, all the build-up, all the whispers and anxieties of the villagers, reduced to a gimmick. It's not just the plot twist, but how it invalidated the film’s already-established framework. It's like spending a fortune on fireworks only to have them fizzle out mid-air. This single, underwhelming twist overshadowed everything that preceded it, turning a potentially great film into a cautionary tale of thematic and narrative miscalculation. Not to mention, the sheer eye-rolling incredulity of the reveal, it just made you want to shout, 'Are you serious?!'.

What’s your favorite movie based on true events? Hmm, that's a tough one. There are so many films claiming to be based on reality. It's always a delicate dance, isn't it? Separating the "based on" from the "inspired by" and the outright fabrications. The beauty of cinema, even those rooted in truth, is the artistic license. I mean, how can you truly capture the essence of a life, a moment, a chain of events, within the confines of a two-hour viewing experience? You're forced to distill, omit, and sometimes, unfortunately, sensationalize. So, with that disclaimer in mind, I’d have to say my favorite is *Catch Me If You Can*. Not because it's the most historically accurate – far from it, I'm sure – but because it captures the spirit of the man, Frank Abagnale Jr., and his almost fantastical escapades.

As a teacher, have you ever been accused of something? As a teacher, have you ever been accused of something?  I’ve never held the title of educator in any formal capacity. I’m more of a student of life, forever learning, perpetually curious. My classroom is the world, and my lessons often come disguised as observations, experiences, and the occasional bout of introspection. Therefore, I haven't faced the brunt of accusations that come with the territory of being a teacher. But, as an avid observer of the human condition, the subject matter of accusations, be they just or unjust, has always piqued my interest. Specifically, the sheer audacity and the intricate dance of blame that accompany them.  One of the most fascinating, yet infuriating, situations I've ever observed unfolded with a close family friend, a woman named Beatrice. She’s a primary school teacher of twenty plus years, and the type of person who genuinely cares for her students. One day, she was accused by a parent of favouritism; supposedly, her son wasn’t getting the same attention as other children in class. Beatrice, ever the optimist, tried to calmly explain her teaching methods, but the parent was relentless. The accusations, fueled by a mixture of insecurity and a dash of entitlement, escalated quickly. They went from not-so-subtle passive-aggressiveness to outright hostility. It was a masterclass in how baseless accusations can be hurled, a clear example of how the accuser, in their own minds, had already declared their 'truth' and would not bend to contrary evidence or reasoned arguments. It was an ugly situation that, unfortunately, many teachers are subject to from time to time.  The incident underscored a few important points: The power of perception, how easily good intentions can be misconstrued, and the exhausting reality that you can't please everyone.

Why do some people not like Coldplay? The question of why anyone might harbor a dislike for Coldplay is, on the surface, relatively straightforward. They’re a band that occupies a unique space in the musical landscape. They are chart-topping, stadium-filling, and seemingly perpetually popular, yet they’re also, to some, insufferably bland, emotionally manipulative, and musically uninspired. The reasons for this disparity in opinion are varied, encompassing both artistic and personal factors. One cannot deny the fact that their music, while undeniably well-produced and polished, often treads a line between sincere and saccharine, a tightrope walk that sometimes plunges into cloying sentimentality. The band’s lyrical content, frequently revolving around themes of love, loss, and existential angst, can come across as generic or even pretentious, especially to those seeking more complex or nuanced storytelling. There’s also the issue of perceived authenticity. In an era dominated by indie bands and artists striving for originality, Coldplay, with their mass-market appeal and relatively safe sound, are often seen as manufactured, a carefully constructed product rather than a genuine artistic expression. Some critics, for instance, dismiss their music as ‘elevator music,’ a background soundtrack designed not to challenge or provoke, but to simply fill the void. But beyond the music itself, other factors come into play, chief among them being the band’s frontman, Chris Martin. His public persona, often perceived as earnest, charming, and at times, a tad self-righteous, can easily grate on those who prefer their rock stars with a touch of arrogance, rebellion, or raw edge. Then there's a phenomenon I would call ‘hipster fatigue,’ that is, a weariness of the constant adoration afforded to them by the mainstream media. Those who pride themselves on their more esoteric tastes might find themselves feeling alienated by a band so readily embraced by the masses. They might simply revel in the fact that they’re not fans. Finally, of course, there’s subjectivity. Music is, after all, inherently subjective. What resonates with one listener might leave another completely cold. For some, Coldplay’s music offers solace, connection, and an emotional catharsis; for others, it simply sounds like a polite, polished, and ultimately forgettable noise. It’s certainly a matter of taste.

What show / movie had no right to be as good as it was? “The Boys” is the show that immediately springs to mind. When I first heard about it, I thought it was going to be another generic superhero caricature, replete with the usual tired tropes and clichés. Yet another attempt to squeeze more blood (pun intended) out of the superhero stone. I was so certain that I was correct in my assessment that I was convinced I would watch it for maybe half an episode. I watched the first three episodes in one sitting. The show is, in short, excellent. I would even go as far as to say it is one of the best shows I have ever seen. And I don't just mean in the superhero genre. What sets “The Boys” apart from the pantheon of run-of-the-mill superhero shows and movies is its unflinching take down of the superhero industrial complex. While other superhero shows are content with using vague ideas of moral ambiguity, “The Boys” treats the subject with a dark sardonic twist. The show seems to revel in the absurdity of the world it has created by displaying the ugly side of the superhero persona. You have the heroes, the mega-corporations that own heroes, the PR teams that clean up the heroes' messes, the fans who are obsessed with the heroes, and yes, even the villains who seem to be almost as reprehensible as the good guys. The show even takes the time to satirize the darker facets of the modern world. They don't just play with these elements. They hold a mirror up to society and force you to laugh at all the ugliness. And I wasn't expecting any of that. I was expecting another show that was trying to be “woke” with shallow social commentary or a movie where the hero suddenly discovers that someone they knew was secretly evil. What I got instead was something smart, insightful, and frequently hilarious. The show's violence is gratuitous, sure, but the show also has heart. So much heart, in fact, that you can forgive the violence. The characters' relationships with each other are well-written, and the acting is top-notch. I would suggest anyone who is interested in an subversive superhero show to give it a watch.

Which actor played a villain role too well for comfort? I’d say for me, it’s Joaquin Phoenix as Commodus in *Gladiator*. Truthfully, there aren't many instances where I feel unsettled watching a film, but seeing Phoenix’s portrayal of the Roman Emperor made my skin crawl. There was something unnervingly real about his performance; it was like watching a viper who relished in its venomous nature. You couldn’t help but hate the guy, not just because he was the antagonist, but because he was a deplorable human being. His sniveling, manipulative, yet profoundly insecure nature was something that was both captivating and distressing to witness. It was a testament to Phoenix’s acting prowess that he could elicit such a visceral response. I was not merely watching a character; I was looking into the abyss of human depravity. He was not just menacing; he was pathetically vile. The way he reveled in his cruelty, the casual way he destroyed the lives of others, the palpable sense of entitlement he possessed. All these things made him not just an effective villain, but a truly disturbing one. Commodus was a villain who transcended fiction and felt horrifyingly close to reality. And that, my friends, is why Phoenix played the role too well for comfort.

What things do people say that make you roll your eyes? It’s funny, isn’t it? How some phrases, repeated ad nauseam, can just instantly trigger that involuntary eye roll. I'm probably guilty of saying some myself, at times, but the ones that really get under my skin are the ones that ooze either passive-aggressive condescension or unearned self-importance. Like when someone feigns concern by saying "Are you sure?" after you’ve made a clear decision, implying that you're clearly a bumbling idiot who needs their implicit guidance. Or, when someone, usually someone with a modicum of privilege, launches into, “Well, *I* would never…” as if their personal preferences are some universal standard of morality or propriety.  Then there are the overused clichés, particularly those that operate as empty platitudes, designed to shut down any actual discussion: “Everything happens for a reason". Really? Is that supposed to offer some consolation when someone dear to you dies tragically? Or how about, "It is what it is?" Yes, Captain Obvious, I’m well aware of the immutable nature of reality, but perhaps I was angling for some genuine advice or empathy. Also, I can't stand it when people declare, "I just want to be happy!" as if happiness is some pre-ordained state achievable with a mere declaration. Sorry, pal, but life is a messy, chaotic, inconsistent rollercoaster ride, not some effortless pursuit of bliss.  But the ultimate eye-roll inducer? The phrase, “I could care less.” It’s always misused. What people actually *mean* to say is "I *couldn't* care less", but yet they use it incorrectly, thus proving, in itself, the very sentiment. The amount of times I have had to bite my tongue as someone utters such a statement is infuriating. It’s also a perfect illustration of the way inane, vapid language can degrade and corrupt the English language, one poorly structured sentence at a time.

What's the most ridiculous thing a coworker told on you to your boss for? I once worked with a woman I shall call "The Oracle". The Oracle was of advanced age, a fixture in the department, and possessed a peculiar blend of wisdom and… let’s say, "opinionatedness." She was the kind of person who knew *everything* about everyone, and wasn't shy about dispensing that knowledge – whether it was wanted or not. The office rumour mill, in the form of The Oracle, was in perpetual operation, and it’s safe to say, everyone was on it, myself very much included. My transgression? Apparently, I possessed the audacity to enjoy a lengthy lunch break.  It started innocently enough. I was on a very tight deadline, and since I was working on a very demanding project I decided to take an extended lunch break to clear my head. I was probably two or three hours late at that point. I went for a long walk, bought a sandwich, and generally tried to de-stress. I came back feeling refreshed and ready to tackle the mountain of work ahead. Unfortunately for me, The Oracle was on duty that day. Upon seeing me return, she summoned me to her desk with a look of grave importance.  “You were gone for three hours,” she stated, her voice a low rumble of disapproval. “The boss is not going to like this. You are being very disrespectful to your superiors and to your coworkers. Many people have to work and work, and you just go gallivanting for three hours.” At that moment it struck me that perhaps The Oracle was secretly hoping for an opportunity to get promoted due to her dedication to keeping the employees in check.  I explained my rationale – the deadline, the project, the need to clear my head. She listened, her expression unyielding, then simply shook her head and issued a stern, "I’m telling the boss." And so, she did. The next day, I was called into my supervisor's office. I anticipated a stern talking-to, maybe even a reprimand. What I wasn’t expecting was the sheer absurdity of the situation. The supervisor, a man known for his laid-back style, was trying his best to suppress a grin.  “So,” he said, leaning back in his chair, “I hear you enjoy extended lunch breaks.” I explained myself again, feeling a blush creep up my neck. He listened, nodding slowly, then made a surprising statement. “Well, The Oracle told me that perhaps you should be fired. But that would not be realistic. The company needs you.” Thus, I somehow escaped The Oracle's wrath. It was, without question, the most ridiculous thing a coworker has ever told on me. The incident cemented her legendary status within the office. And on days she was absent the office experienced complete chaos.

What red flag did you have right before a job offer that you wish you had heeded? Truth be told, I have a penchant for ignoring red flags, especially if there's the slightest promise of getting ahead. This is something I've had to actively work on over the years, but even with that conscious effort, I've still stumbled. Case in point: during my brief stint as a media consultant. Fresh out of university, starry-eyed and eager to "make a name for myself," I was offered what seemed like a dream gig at a burgeoning PR firm. The job promised exposure, a competitive salary, and the opportunity to work with high-profile clients. The interview process had been gruelling, a multi-stage marathon of personality tests, case studies, and panel discussions. I thought I'd aced them all. During my final interview, however, there was a moment, a tiny discordant note that I should've paid more attention to, but which I, in my eagerness, brushed aside. The CEO, a charismatic but undeniably arrogant man, spent a significant portion of the interview talking about the "competitive nature" of the industry and how "mediocrity wouldn't be tolerated". He also made a point of emphasizing the long hours and demanding workload. My red flag was his constant references to 'teamwork' yet he continually used the words ‘I’ and ‘me’ in every sentence. Now, in retrospect, that should have been a screaming siren. It spoke of a top-down structure, a lack of appreciation for employees, and an environment where individual ambition would be prized above all else. Yet, I was so caught up in the aura of the office, the promise of prestige, and the potential payday that I chose to ignore it. As I sat there, nodding and smiling, I convinced myself that I was tough enough, driven enough, to thrive in such a cutthroat world and that all of this ‘teamwork’ talk was simply industry lingo. Within a few weeks of starting that job, it was clear that my initial instincts had been correct. The environment turned out to be as toxic as I had feared. The long hours, the unrelenting pressure, and the constant backstabbing took a heavy toll. The CEO's leadership style was, to put it mildly, dictatorial. I was miserable. I ended up resigning after just four months, wiser, definitely poorer, and with a healthy dose of cynicism. These days, I'm more attuned to those subtle warning signs. I've learned to trust my gut, which is to say, I ask more probing questions and do more background research. It's a lesson I had to learn the hard way, but I’m better for it, I suppose.

What is an unpopular opinion you hold? That depends on the circle, doesn't it? In some Trinidadian circles, I imagine my views would be downright heretical. Being a relatively well-read, tech-savvy, left-leaning individual, I often find myself at odds with the prevailing sentiments of my society. To be frank, I'm quite aware of the unpopular opinions I hold, and the fact that I don’t constantly trumpet them from the rooftops is more a reflection of my innate disinclination for conflict and confrontation more than a genuine fear of disapproval. One such opinion, which I've been loath to share with my more conservative relatives, is my staunch belief in the efficacy of secularism. Given that Trinidad is a land steeped in religious fervor, advocating for a separation of church and state is akin to spitting in the face of the Holy Trinity (or whatever deity you happen to believe in). It's a topic that's frequently met with scorn, dismissal, or at best, a weary tolerance. Similarly, my unwavering support for LGBTQ+ rights is another viewpoint that tends to ruffle a few feathers. While the legal landscape has improved over recent years, societal attitudes remain stubbornly resistant to progress. My open embrace of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities is often met with raised eyebrows, hushed whispers, and the occasional outright condemnation.

What is that one picture that describes the lowest point in your life? There’s no single image that can encapsulate the nadir of existence, but if I were forced to choose, it would undoubtedly be a photo from my turbulent period of chronic migraines. Picture this: I’m sprawled on the bathroom floor, the cold tile a frigid comfort against my throbbing skull. The fluorescent light above is a sadistic spotlight, amplifying the agony. My face is contorted, a grotesque mask of pain, mouth agape in a silent scream. My eyes – those once vibrant windows to the soul – are bloodshot and swollen, barely able to focus, let alone comprehend the torturous reality of the moment. A half-empty bottle of water lies discarded nearby, a testament to my failed attempts at self-care. The sterile white walls of the bathroom seem to shrink, closing in on me, suffocating me with a suffocating sense of despair. My entire being is consumed by a relentless, unrelenting ache – a physical manifestation of the emotional and mental torment I was enduring at the time. The very air feels heavy, thick with the scent of despair and failure. It’s a picture of utter vulnerability, a stark reminder of the debilitating power of migraines. It represents a time when I felt utterly lost, adrift in a sea of pain, with no safe harbor in sight. It's a visual echo of the lowest point in my life. The memory of that moment, that image, is enough to send shivers down my spine even now.

Whom did you feel bad for in high school? As a skinny, awkward teenager, high school felt like navigating a minefield of social landmines. I wasn't particularly popular, nor was I a pariah. I existed in a sort of purgatorial middle ground, flitting between cliques and trying to find my place in the convoluted hierarchy that is adolescence. Truthfully, I felt bad for almost everyone at some point. The jocks, perpetually worried about their image and performance; the preps, suffocated by familial expectations and social pressures; the misfits, ostracized for their differences – each carried a burden of their own making, or one imposed upon them. But the person I felt the most sympathy for, and the one who's story sticks with me still, was a girl named Sarah. She was a year my senior, and stunningly beautiful. Bright, witty, and possessing a sharp intelligence, Sarah should have been the queen of the school. Instead, she was quietly battling a debilitating eating disorder, hidden beneath layers of makeup and forced smiles.

Which supporting actress was much more memorable than the star of a movie? This is always a difficult question to answer, as it’s entirely subjective, but there are a few that readily spring to mind. Often, the supporting cast is given a much freer hand in terms of character portrayal. They aren’t saddled with the pressures of carrying the entire film, so they’re given the freedom to be more nuanced, more eccentric. The lead actor or actress has to balance the constraints of maintaining their star persona, which can at times be rather stifling. It's not their fault - that’s just how the game is played. Supporting actors get to be themselves and the result is usually electrifying.  One example that comes immediately to mind is Lena Heady’s performance as Queen Gorgo in *300*. I mean, I loved Gerard Butler in it – he certainly looked the part of a fierce Spartan warrior – but Heady’s Gorgo was a colossus of her own making. She made a few short appearances throughout the movie, but every scene containing her was masterfully conceived and perfectly executed. Her charisma was undeniable, her dialogue as sharp as a Spartan spear. The supporting role was much more gripping than the hero.

What is the scariest moment you have had in your own home? Like most of the middle-class families in Trinidad, my family lived a life of relative comfort, devoid of any serious physical threats. We lived in a quiet suburban area and our house stood just outside the busy city areas. So, in my childhood and teens, the idea of being in danger in my own home was something that I mostly got from the movies and a handful of true crime shows that my mother and her friends watched. We were simply not in the realm of any real danger. Burglaries were rare and petty, and violent crime was something that happened in bad neighbourhoods, not ours. But I still had my share of nightmares, especially as I slowly weaned myself off of Disney and began dabbling into the horror genre. I loved horror movies, but my mind could be a bit susceptible to the images of the things that I witnessed on screen. I’d often find myself staring at the shadows, and every creak of the house would sound like a lurking intruder. My parents, bless their hearts, were also somewhat wary of the stories that I had imagined. They knew of my penchant for the lurid, and they often told me to settle down and turn off the television. Anyway, one night, when I was around my mid-teens, I was home alone. My parents and my sister had gone to visit some relatives that lived on the other side of the island. I relished such nights because I had the house to myself, and I could watch anything I wanted, eat anything I wanted and play my music as loud as I wanted. As such, I decided to have a monster movie marathon. The plan was well laid out and well executed. I made some popcorn and got a couple of soft drinks. At about midnight I placed the last movie in the VHS player and got ready to enjoy myself. All was fine and dandy and even the occasional jump scare of the movie didn't bother me. But at some point during the film, the TV shut off, a common occurrence brought on by voltage fluctuations. I was momentarily annoyed until I realised that the TV didn’t make its familiar click sound like it normally did when the voltage fluctuated. I immediately got the fear. This feeling was compounded when, shortly thereafter, all the lights in the house went out. I wasn’t surprised to be plunged in darkness but what startled me was that the house was eerily silent. My first instinct was to ignore it, assume it was the result of some momentary power outage and wait for the electricity to return. But the more I waited, the more I realised that it wasn’t. There were no car or truck sounds outside, even though the front of our house was located on a relatively busy road. Even more unsettling was the silence of the crickets and other night insects. Our house normally had those sounds. I tip-toed out of my room and started to walk around the house with a flashlight. I was terrified. I called out for my parents. No answer. I peered through the blinds to see if there was any signs of something unusual. Nothing. The silence was now beginning to drive me mad. I started to feel like I was in a horror movie and that something or someone was in the house with me. Then it happened. Silence was shattered, and the front door began to slowly creek open as if being pushed by some unseen force. I froze. I stood there paralysed. I waited there, frozen, for what seemed like an eternity.

Can you provide some examples of average actors delivering great performances due to well-written characters? One of the most ubiquitous examples that pops into mind is Javier Bardem as Anton Chigurh in *No Country for Old Men*. Anyone who saw this film and has seen Bardem’s other work can attest to the fact that he is a very good actor, but in this movie, he was transcendent. Chigurh, a remorseless killer with a disturbingly simple philosophy, could have easily been a one-dimensional villain. But the Coen Brothers crafted a character whose motivations, though unsettling, were undeniably clear. Bardem’s performance, perfectly capturing the character’s stoic demeanor, unsettling gaze, and unsettlingly deliberate delivery, elevated a well-written character to an icon of modern cinema. Another compelling example is Christoph Waltz as Colonel Hans Landa in Quentin Tarantino's *Inglourious Basterds*. You get the sense that Waltz is a talented actor, but a bit of a journeyman. He’s capable and competent, but never really blew anyone away with his acting. Then along comes Tarantino with a character who is a multilingual, intelligent, manipulative, and utterly terrifying Nazi officer. Waltz, armed with a brilliantly crafted script, delivers a performance that is both charming and chilling. He effortlessly switches between languages, his eyes twinkling with a dark humor. The audience, like the characters in the film, is completely enthralled and also scared of him. Both Bardem and Waltz's performances demonstrate the power of a well-written character.

Have you ever had a co-worker who you worked closely with get fired for something truly shocking that you never saw coming? As a matter of fact, yes. It wasn't just any co-worker; it was my manager, a suave, impeccably dressed gentleman named Mr. Harrison. I should mention that at the time, I was working in the IT department of a rather prominent local bank, a place where adherence to rules was paramount, and any transgression was met with swift, decisive action. Mr. Harrison, however, had always struck me as the epitome of professionalism, a man of unwavering integrity. He was the type who always had a witty remark up his sleeve, a reassuring presence in the face of any technical crisis. He exuded an air of sophistication that made you believe he could handle anything that came his way. I'd always admired his calm demeanor, his ability to navigate the often-turbulent waters of corporate politics with grace and finesse.  The event that led to his dismissal unfolded with unsettling speed. It started subtly enough, with hushed whispers and furtive glances around the office. Then came the abrupt summoning of Mr. Harrison to the executive suite, followed by his swift return, his face a mask of forced composure. We sensed that something was amiss, but we couldn't have fully predicted how wrong things were. No one knew what was happening until a notice from HR was sent around; he'd been terminated. The reason cited was "gross misconduct." Gross misconduct? This was the man who was always there for me when the network went down in a critical moment. The only thing I could muster was, how the hell? To this day, I am baffled as to what “gross misconduct” means. Mr. Harrison? It was almost impossible to fathom how. The rumors began to fly, filling the office with a frenzied mix of speculation and gossip. It turned out that Mr. Harrison had embezzled funds from the bank, siphoning off significant sums over several months. The shock was profound, bordering on disbelief. To add to this, what was even more shocking was the fact that this professional with years of experience had been caught by a rookie, right out of university, who was working in the finance department on a one month internship, a woman whose name I am not going to say. I, and most of my co-workers, simply could not reconcile the image of our seemingly flawless manager with the reality of his actions. It was a harsh lesson, a stark reminder of the fallibility of even the most seemingly trustworthy individuals.

If all animals were horse-sized, which would be the most majestic to ride into battle? This is difficult to answer because the animal to mount into battle would depend on the role it has to play. If it's a slow-moving, highly armoured, tank-like role, then perhaps a horse-sized tortoise or armadillo. If the role is to ferry supplies and troops across land regardless of how dangerous, then a horse-sized elephant. However, the animal who looks the most visually majestic to ride into battle, in my humble opinion, would have to be a horse-sized lion. Imagine the sight of such a creature clad in shining armour, its mane billowing in the wind, its roars echoing across the battlefield, its massive claws tearing through enemy ranks. A lion, the king of the jungle, amplified to the scale of a horse, is the definition of raw power and untamed elegance. The mere sight of it would be enough to demoralize any enemy. A lion exudes an aura of dominance, a primal ferocity that's unmatched in the animal kingdom. Its sleek, powerful form, the glint in its predatory eyes, the sheer presence it commands – these are the elements of true majesty. As it charges towards the enemy, its muscles rippling beneath its fearsome visage, it would be a sight to behold. A majestic, terrifying embodiment of nature’s fury, a creature that would inspire awe and terror in equal measure. Indeed, no other animal could hope to match the leonine combination of grace, power, and sheer dominating presence on the battlefield. Picture yourself riding such a creature, you wouldn't just be fighting, you'd be conquering not only the enemy but also the very concept of death itself. The king of beasts, amplified to equine proportions, is not just a mount but rather a symbol of indomitable will.

What is the most obnoxious thing you have seen someone do at the grocery store? I've witnessed a litany of offenses in the hallowed aisles of the grocery store, each a minor affront to my sensibilities. But one particular incident rises above the rest in terms of pure, unadulterated obnoxiousness. It happened a few years ago – feels like a lifetime, actually – and I still shudder when I think about it. I was patiently waiting in the express checkout line, the one with the "10 items or less" sign. As usual, it was clogged with slow-moving customers, each meticulously examining their produce before finally handing it over to the cashier. A veritable symphony of sighs, and the gentle *beep* of the scanner at its regular pace. Suddenly, a woman, perhaps in her late fifties, breezed in, pushing a cart overflowing with items. And I mean *overflowing*. It was a genuine mountain of groceries. She glanced at the sign, then looked at the cashier, gave a dismissive chuckle, and proceeded to unload her haul onto the conveyor belt. The cashier, bless her soul, looked utterly defeated, but knew she couldn't say anything. The woman then started acting like she was the star of her own personal show. Each item received a dramatic pause, a scrutinising examination, presumably for any sign of imperfection. The line behind me began to grow. Murmurs of disapproval started to bubble up from the assembled masses of shoppers. A young mother with a screaming toddler gave the woman a withering look. But did she care? Not a damn bit. She was too engrossed in her own self-importance to notice the petty turmoil she caused. The sheer audacity of her actions was enough to send me into a state of silent, seething rage. It was a display of flagrant disregard for the rules, for common decency, and for everyone else's time. It was, in a word, obnoxious. The woman eventually finished, paid, and exited the store, leaving a trail of frustrated shoppers in her wake. I, meanwhile, was left with a lingering feeling of bewilderment. Where did she get the nerve? What made her think her time was more valuable than everyone else's? It remains a mystery that continues to perplex me. And that, dear readers, is the most obnoxious thing I've ever seen at the grocery store.

What is the lamest “benefit” you’ve been offered by an employer? I have worked a fair share of odd jobs in my life, mainly to fund my tuition fees or to simply find some extra pocket money on the side. As such I’ve encountered companies offering a plethora of “benefits” to lure me on board. I’ve seen it all: the free coffee, the ping pong tables, the pool tables, the Friday afternoon beer sessions, the monthly all you can eat breakfasts and the occasional company barbeque. Most of the time I would laugh about the ridiculousness of it all and then promptly refuse the job offers. However there was this one instance that takes the cake. I was in the penultimate year of my degree and I needed some real income to fund a rather crucial thesis. The job advertised was for a cashier at a local supermarket chain at a starting salary of $3000 a month. I thought that was a bit too low since I was coming away with $2000 a month at the time but I went anyway. Upon arriving I was surprised as to the scale of the place. It was HUGE, filled with almost every product you can imagine. This was the biggest supermarket on the island. It was filled to the brim with customers. The sheer amount of people in the shop was unbelievable. I was slightly intimidated. After all, I had only worked behind the till a handful of times. I had a brief interview with a middle aged lady who was the HR manager. She was friendly and enthusiastic as she explained the functions of the role. I was even more surprised when she told me the salary was actually $3500 a month. An additional $500 was a sizeable boost. The catch? As she explained, you would have to “earn” it as you go. She elaborated in detail the performance metrics. The more you perform, the higher the salary. As she ended her explanation, she looked in the most pleasant way possible and told me about the additional benefits. “We offer a flexible schedule which is determined by your performance! You can tell us whether you would like to work a full day or half a day.” I sat upright to pay closer attention. My ears perked up. I thought to myself, “Wow, that’s convenient!” The HR manager then continued: “And, most importantly you get a staff discount on ALL products in the shop! So if you are buying some groceries….you can receive a steep discount.” I paused. I scratched my head. I knew what was coming. “The maximum discount?”, I asked. “10%”, she replied with an eager smile. I laughed. I told her that I would call her. The biggest supermarket on the island was trying to entice me with a measly 10% discount on its shelves. I told her my current job offered a 20% discount. I rejected the offer and felt a little sorry for her and walked away.

At what age did you stop enjoying YA fiction? That’s a loaded question, innit? The sort that has me contemplating the very nature of time, memory, and the elusive concept of “enjoyment” itself. If I'm being honest, I've never been a devout follower of Young Adult fiction. I have never been on that bandwagon. There was a time when I thought I was, you know. I’d read a few books that fell vaguely within the genre, like *The Hunger Games* or a handful of John Green's novels, figuring they were the literary equivalent of fast food – quick, easy, and vaguely satisfying while you’re consuming it. But just like cheap take-out, they didn’t stick with me. They didn't leave a lasting taste in my mouth. They didn’t provide the nourishment for my literary cravings. My true literary loves all reside in much loftier realms. Now don’t get me wrong; I’m not knocking the genre entirely. YA fiction does serve a purpose. It introduces teenagers to the world of reading. It gives them something to connect with. It often tackles important themes in a format that's easily digestible. However, the tropes, the melodramatic romance, the all-too-convenient plot devices… they get old, quick. They start to grate on the nerves. Ultimately, it’s an invitation for me to groan, roll my eyes, and toss the book aside in favor of something with a bit more substance, something that actually makes me think. So, at what age did I stop enjoying YA fiction? I'd say I never really did, to begin with.
